vjimc-1997-cat1-01.title: Legendre symbol of $-2$
vjimc-1997-cat1-01.body:
Let $d$ be a positive divisor of $a^2+2$. Since $a$ is odd, $a^2+2$ is odd, so $d$ and all its prime factors are odd.

**Primes.** Let $p$ be a prime with $p\mid a^2+2$. Then $p$ is odd and $a^2\equiv-2\pmod p$. Also $p\nmid a$, since otherwise $p\mid2$. So $-2$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$, i.e. $\left(\frac{-2}{p}\right)=1$. By the supplementary laws of quadratic reciprocity,
$$\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}2},\qquad\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{p^2-1}8}.$$
Check the odd residues mod 8:

| $p\bmod 8$ | $\left(\frac{-1}p\right)$ | $\left(\frac2p\right)$ | $\left(\frac{-2}p\right)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $+1$ | $+1$ | $+1$ |
| 3 | $-1$ | $-1$ | $+1$ |
| 5 | $+1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ |
| 7 | $-1$ | $+1$ | $-1$ |

Hence $p\equiv1$ or $3\pmod 8$.

**General $d$.** $d$ is a product of primes dividing $a^2+2$, each $\equiv1$ or $3\pmod8$ ($d=1$ is the empty product, $\equiv1$). The set $\{1,3\}\subset\mathbb Z/8$ is closed under multiplication: $1\cdot1=1$, $1\cdot3=3$, $3\cdot3=9\equiv1$. By induction on the number of prime factors, $d\equiv1$ or $3\pmod 8$. ∎

vjimc-1997-cat1-02.title: A monotone combination, then a contraction
vjimc-1997-cat1-02.body:
Put $\beta=1-\alpha\in[0,1)$ and, for $n\ge2$,
$$w_n=a_n+\beta a_{n-1}.$$

**$w_n$ is non-increasing.** By the hypothesis,
$$w_{n+1}=a_{n+1}+\beta a_n\le(\alpha a_n+\beta a_{n-1})+\beta a_n=a_n+\beta a_{n-1}=w_n,$$
using $\alpha+\beta=1$. Since $(a_n)$ is bounded, so is $(w_n)$. Hence $w_n\to W$ for some $W\in\mathbb R$.

**$a_n$ converges.** Let $c=\frac{W}{1+\beta}$ and $e_n=a_n-c$. Then $a_n=w_n-\beta a_{n-1}$ gives
$$e_n=w_n-\beta a_{n-1}-c=(w_n-W)-\beta(a_{n-1}-c)=\delta_n-\beta e_{n-1},$$
where $\delta_n=w_n-W\to0$ (we used $W-\beta c-c=W-(1+\beta)c=0$). Let $E=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|e_n|$, which is finite because $(a_n)$ is bounded. From $|e_n|\le|\delta_n|+\beta|e_{n-1}|$ we get, taking $\limsup$,
$$E\le0+\beta E,$$
so $(1-\beta)E\le0$. Since $1-\beta=\alpha>0$, this gives $E=0$. Hence $e_n\to0$, i.e.
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=\frac{W}{1+\beta}=\frac{W}{2-\alpha}.$$
∎

vjimc-1997-cat1-02.title: Using $\limsup$ and $\liminf$
vjimc-1997-cat1-02.body:
Let $L=\limsup a_n$ and $l=\liminf a_n$ (finite by boundedness). Suppose $l<L$.

First, $a_{n+1}\le\max(a_n,a_{n-1})$, since the right side of the hypothesis is a convex combination. So $b_n=\max(a_n,a_{n-1})$ is non-increasing, and it converges to $L$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ with $\alpha(L-l)>3\varepsilon$, and choose $n_0$ with $a_n<L+\varepsilon$ for $n\ge n_0$. Since $a_m$ comes within $\varepsilon$ of $l$ for infinitely many $m$, pick $m\ge n_0+1$ with $a_m<l+\varepsilon$. Then
$$a_{m+1}\le\alpha a_m+(1-\alpha)a_{m-1}<\alpha(l+\varepsilon)+(1-\alpha)(L+\varepsilon)=L+\varepsilon-\alpha(L-l)<L-2\varepsilon .$$
Hence $b_{m+1}=\max(a_{m+1},a_m)<\max(L-2\varepsilon,\ l+\varepsilon)$. Since $l+\varepsilon<L-2\varepsilon$ (because $L-l>3\varepsilon/\alpha\ge3\varepsilon$), we get $b_{m+1}<L-2\varepsilon$. As $(b_n)$ is non-increasing, $b_n<L-2\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge m+1$, contradicting $b_n\to L$.

Therefore $l=L$, and the bounded sequence converges. ∎

vjimc-1997-cat1-03.title: Logarithmic derivative and Leibniz's rule
vjimc-1997-cat1-03.body:
Write $p_m=c_1^m+\dots+c_n^m>0$ ($m\ge1$). Near $x=0$ all factors $1-c_jx$ are positive, so $f>0$ there and $f$ is smooth ($C^\infty$) near $0$. Let
$$g(x)=\ln f(x)=-\sum_{j=1}^n\ln(1-c_jx).$$

**Derivatives of $g$.** Differentiating, $g'(x)=\sum_j\frac{c_j}{1-c_jx}$, and by induction
$$g^{(m)}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{(m-1)!\,c_j^m}{(1-c_jx)^m}\qquad(m\ge1).$$
Hence $g^{(m)}(0)=(m-1)!\,p_m>0$ for every $m\ge1$.

**Derivatives of $f$.** Since $f=e^{g}$, we have $f'=f\,g'$. Differentiating $k$ times with Leibniz's rule,
$$f^{(k+1)}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom ki f^{(i)}\,g^{(k+1-i)} .$$
Now induct on $k$. We have $f(0)=1>0$, and $f'(0)=f(0)g'(0)=p_1>0$. If $f(0),f'(0),\dots,f^{(k)}(0)$ are all positive, then at $x=0$ every term on the right is a product of positive numbers, so $f^{(k+1)}(0)>0$.

Hence $f^{(k)}(0)>0$ for all $k\ge1$. ∎

vjimc-1997-cat1-03.title: Power series with positive coefficients
vjimc-1997-cat1-03.body:
Let $R=1/\max_j|c_j|$ (or $R=\infty$ if all $c_j=0$; that case is excluded since $p_1>0$). For $|x|<R$,
$$g(x)=-\sum_j\ln(1-c_jx)=\sum_j\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{(c_jx)^m}{m}=\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{p_m}{m}x^m ,$$
where all series converge absolutely. So $g$ is a power series with strictly positive coefficients and $g(0)=0$.

Then $f=e^g=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{g^r}{r!}$. Expanding each power $g^r$ gives a power series with non-negative coefficients. Everything converges absolutely for $|x|$ small (the majorant $e^{\tilde g(|x|)}$ with $\tilde g(t)=\sum_m\frac{|p_m|}{m}t^m$ is finite), so we may collect terms. The coefficient of $x^k$ in $f$ is therefore at least its coefficient in the $r=1$ term $g$, namely $\frac{p_k}{k}>0$.

By uniqueness of Taylor coefficients, $f^{(k)}(0)=k!\,[x^k]f\ge k!\,\frac{p_k}{k}>0$. ∎

vjimc-1997-cat1-04m.title: Group by number of digits
vjimc-1997-cat1-04m.body:
Group the terms by the number of digits. Let $B_m=\sum_{10^{m-1}\le n<10^m}\frac{a^{f(n)}}{n^2}$ for $m\ge1$.

**Counting.** An $m$-digit number has a nonzero leading digit (9 choices), followed by $m-1$ digits. The number of $m$-digit $n$ with exactly $j$ zeros is $9\binom{m-1}{j}9^{m-1-j}$: choose the $j$ zero positions among the last $m-1$ digits, then fill the other $m-1-j$ positions with nonzero digits. Hence, by the binomial theorem,
$$\sum_{10^{m-1}\le n<10^m}a^{f(n)}=9\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\binom{m-1}{j}a^j9^{m-1-j}=9(9+a)^{m-1}.$$

**Bounds.** For these $n$, $10^{2(m-1)}\le n^2<10^{2m}$, so
$$\frac{9(9+a)^{m-1}}{100^{m}}\le B_m\le\frac{9(9+a)^{m-1}}{100^{m-1}} ,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \frac{9}{100}q^{m-1}\le B_m\le9q^{m-1},\qquad q=\frac{9+a}{100}.$$

**Conclusion.** The series has positive terms, so it converges iff $\sum_mB_m$ converges. By the comparison test with the geometric series $\sum q^{m-1}$, this happens iff $q<1$, i.e. $a<91$. For $a\ge91$ the lower bound gives $B_m\ge\frac9{100}$ for all $m$, so the series diverges.

**Answer:** the series converges exactly for $0<a<91$. ∎
